GitHub Actions install tests

Source: vignettes/dev-github-actions-install-tests.Rmd
dev-github-actions-install-tests.Rmd

This note explains the GitHub Actions workflows that check whether EJAM can be installed. These workflows are intentionally separate from R CMD check because they answer different questions.

Shared Arrow/curl check

Every install job described below runs .github/scripts/check-arrow-curl-deps.R. That script checks that:

  • DESCRIPTION declares arrow (>= 24.0.0) and curl (>= 7.1.0)
  • the installed arrow and curl packages meet those minimums
  • the system libcurl is at least 7.73.0
  • arrow can write a small Arrow file and read it back unchanged

Quick install check

Workflow file: .github/workflows/install-quick-check.yaml

This is the low-cost install check. It runs one job, on Ubuntu with the current release of R. Its steps:

  1. Install a few system libraries with apt-get (cmake, libcurl, OpenSSL, pkg-config).
  2. Install EJAM’s hard R package dependencies (Depends, Imports, LinkingTo) with r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies, plus pak and testthat.
  3. Run the shared Arrow/curl check.
  4. Install EJAM with pak (see the install sources below).
  5. Load EJAM with library(EJAM).
  6. Run two test files, test-zip-api-wrappers.R and test-ejamit-zip-alias.R.

Automatic triggers, which always use the github-sha install source:

  • push to main or development
  • pull request to main or development

Manual trigger:

  • workflow_dispatch, with install_source set to either local (the default) or github-sha

Install sources:

  • local: installs the checked-out source tree with pak::local_install(".", dependencies = FALSE). It proves the source tree installs.
  • github-sha: installs from GitHub by commit SHA with pak::pkg_install("OWNER/REPO@SHA", dependencies = NA). It proves the same commit can be installed from GitHub. For a pull request, this is the pull request’s latest commit, from the repository the pull request comes from.

Use the manual trigger when a branch changes package dependencies, installation code, or workflow files and you want a quick install check without running the release checks below.

Release and user install checks

Workflow file: .github/workflows/install-release-user-check.yaml

This workflow is deliberately more expensive. It is for release validation and for testing installation paths that users are likely to use. It has two jobs, described below: the prepared-runner matrix and the clean-machine pak install.

What runs depends on how the workflow starts:

How it starts test_scope What runs Jobs
push of a tag matching v* (none) the prepared-runner matrix 18
GitHub Release published (none) the clean-machine pak install 2
manual user-style (default) the clean-machine pak install 2
manual full-matrix the prepared-runner matrix 18
manual both both jobs 20
manual ubuntu-only the Ubuntu rows of the prepared-runner matrix 6

ubuntu-only runs all three install methods on both R versions without using any Windows or macOS runners.

Manual runs take three inputs:

  • ref: the branch, tag, or commit SHA to install and test, such as development or v4.2024.0
  • expected_version (optional): the version that ref should have, matching Version in its DESCRIPTION, such as 4.2024.0
  • test_scope: one of the four choices in the table above

Both jobs check the version the same way, using the ref being tested (the ref input, or the tag for a tag push or a published release):

  • If expected_version is filled in, the version must match it.
  • If it is blank and the ref looks like a release tag (v followed by a digit, such as v4.2024.0), the version must match the tag without its v (4.2024.0).
  • Otherwise, for a branch or commit SHA, the version is not checked.

So a manual run on a tag needs no expected_version. Fill it in to check the version of a branch or SHA.

Prepared-runner matrix (full-matrix)

This job tests Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS, with oldrel-1 and release R, and three install methods, for 18 combinations:

  • local: install the checked-out source tree with utils::install.packages()
  • github-ref: install from GitHub by branch, tag, or SHA with remotes::install_github()
  • url-tarball: install GitHub’s source archive (.tar.gz) for that ref with remotes::install_url()

Before installing EJAM, each job prepares the runner the way a developer’s machine would be prepared:

  • On Ubuntu, it installs system libraries with apt-get (GDAL, GEOS, PROJ, udunits, cairo, and others).
  • On macOS, it installs system libraries with Homebrew (GDAL, cairo, udunits, freetype, and others).
  • On Windows, it installs no system libraries.
  • On every runner, it installs EJAM’s hard R package dependencies from DESCRIPTION (Depends, Imports, LinkingTo, and their own dependencies) using r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies with dependencies: '"hard"', which uses pak internally. It also installs remotes. Packages listed only under Suggests are not installed.

Each job then runs these steps:

  1. The shared Arrow/curl check.
  2. The version check described above, applied to Version in the checked-out DESCRIPTION, before EJAM is installed.
  3. Install EJAM with install.packages() or remotes, not pak, using INSTALL_opts = c("--with-keep.source", "--install-tests", "--no-test-load"). pak::pkg_install() is preferred for ordinary user installs, but it does not accept those R CMD INSTALL options.
  4. Load EJAM with library(EJAM).

A pass here shows that EJAM’s source installs and loads on each platform, given its dependencies. It does not show that a new user can get those dependencies.

Clean-machine pak install (user-style)

This job tests Windows and macOS with the current release of R. It skips every preparation step above: no Homebrew libraries and no setup-r-dependencies. It starts from a plain R installation and follows the installation instructions:

options(timeout = 600)
install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("Public-Environmental-Data-Partners/EJAM@REF",
                 dependencies = NA, upgrade = FALSE)
library(EJAM)

dependencies = NA installs the hard dependencies (Depends, Imports, LinkingTo), not Suggests, which matches the installation instructions.

For a manual run, REF is the ref workflow input. For a GitHub Release published event, REF is that release’s tag, for example v4.2024.0.

After loading EJAM, the job applies the version check described above to the installed version of EJAM. It then runs the shared Arrow/curl check.

This job catches problems the prepared-runner matrix cannot see, because those problems happen while dependencies are installed:

  • It installs EJAM itself from GitHub with pak, the way users are told to. The prepared-runner matrix uses pak only for dependencies and installs EJAM with install.packages() or remotes.
  • On macOS, every dependency must install without Homebrew libraries. That works when CRAN has ready-built (binary) packages for the current R. A dependency that has to be compiled from source, for example right after a new R release, can fail here even though it passes in the prepared-runner matrix.

If the prepared-runner matrix passes and this job fails, look first at dependencies and pak, not at EJAM’s own code.

What neither job tests

Both jobs install only hard dependencies, so neither installs the packages listed only under Suggests. These include the GitHub-only packages in DESCRIPTION’s Remotes: field (ACSdownload and AOI), so neither job tests installing them. Neither job runs EJAM’s tests or checks the functions and vignettes that need Suggests packages. --install-tests only copies the tests into the installed package without running them. R CMD check covers those.

What each trigger proves

  • A tag push proves that the tag’s DESCRIPTION has the tag’s version, and that the tag installs and loads by local source, GitHub ref, and GitHub source archive, on all three operating systems and both R versions.
  • A published release proves that the release’s tag installs with the public pak-based instructions on Windows and macOS, and that the installed version matches the tag.
  • A manual run can test a branch, tag, or SHA before deciding whether to create or publish a release.

Branches and workflow file versions

Automatic runs use the workflow file from the commit that triggered them. For example, a tag push uses the workflow file in the tagged commit.

Manual runs involve two different choices on the Actions page:

  • Use workflow from picks the branch or tag whose copy of the workflow file runs. That copy decides which inputs and test_scope choices exist. Current branches share the same workflow file, so leave this on main. Older release tags have older copies of the workflow, which may lack some choices, such as ubuntu-only.
  • The ref input picks what is installed and tested. It can be any branch, tag, or SHA, and does not need to contain the workflow file.

GitHub shows the Run workflow button only for workflows that exist on the repository’s default branch (main). Once that is true, any branch can be chosen under Use workflow from. In practice, keep workflow files as similar as possible in development, main, and the active preparation branch unless there is a deliberate reason for a branch-specific workflow.

Recommended workflow promotion:

  • Edit and test workflow changes on the active working branch first.
  • Integrate vX workflow changes into vX.20YY.0-prep first. Keep development on the current version line until team authorizes the version change/transition.
  • At that transition, bring the approved changes into development, then main through the release process before relying on them for release validation.
  • For historical install checks, select an existing release tag rather than maintaining a separate branch per data vintage.

The branch workflow proves only that its branch or commit installs as the version in DESCRIPTION. It does not prove that a release tag installs until that tag exists and its tag-triggered workflow passes. In particular, the preparation branch name does not activate v4 data or change its package version.
